### 2026-10-11 – Okay back at it. Turns out my dad was right about the labels, but that wasn't even the only thing going on.

**4h**

Okay back at it. Turns out my dad was right about the labels, but that wasn't even the only thing going on.

First, 5CL really was a typo for SCL (whoops). And the buttons were lowercase gpio2 and gpio3 while the ESP32 had capital GPIO2 and GPIO3, and KiCad actually  cares about uppercase vs lowercase!

 ALSO I realized I made the section titles like "Buttons" and "Oled" using the net label tool (L) instead of the normal text tool (T), so KiCad literally  thought the word "Buttons" was an electrical wire floating in space with nothing plugged into it lol.

  Fixed the typos, changed the titles to normal text, drew actual wires from the switch pins to the labels, and hit save.

![step1_schematic_fixed](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/SbrkIUQC9RUO8DToeavOMkE0vX78Rnig/b12b24223b2b40878b574dffc88125eb67a081e4fb2f653f08b339acd3328101.png)

  Hit F8 to update the PCB from schematic and nice!! The thin blue guideline lines finally showed up connecting to the ESP32 pins.

  I tried drawing a red trace from the resistor down towards the chip, but then I looked at the screen and freaked out because almost EVERY single pin had a
  yellow arrow pointing at it.

![step2_drc_yellow_arrows](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/SbrkIUQC9RUO8DToeavOMkE0vX78Rnig/94bff20fe589283916794053465c8f2fff21fc8aefa35a10ffa19a9d580f9f8e.png)

  I thought my whole board was broken. But turns out the yellow arrows were just DRC warning markers left on the screen from earlier! Most of them were just
  KiCad complaining that the white silkscreen outline on the ESP32 footprint touches the solder mask of the pads. The guide literally said "you can ignore any
  warnings", so I opened the DRC window, hit "Delete All Markers", and poof, all the yellow arrows vanished.

  Next problem: my trace from R1 was stretching all the way across the board because I had put U1 (the blue DHT11 sensor) way down at the bottom of the star! In
  the guide's picture it sits right under R1 at the top point. Moved U1 up to the top next to R1.

  Then I learned about the Ground Pour trick. You draw a filled zone on the back copper (B.Cu) set to GND, wrap it around the whole board, and hit B. KiCad
  floods the entire back with copper and it connected ALL 7 GND pins automatically without me having to draw a single trace for ground! That felt like a cheat
  code.

  After that, replaced my "rustic" star outline with the actual clean pixel star on Edge.Cuts, routed the rest of the traces on front and back copper, and ran
  DRC.

  0 unconnected items!! Only the 2 courtyard errors on J1 that the guide told us to ignore.

  And check out the 3D render... THIS LOOKS SO SICK!

![step3_starbie_3d_top](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/SbrkIUQC9RUO8DToeavOMkE0vX78Rnig/d2b8f437daf5b7144ef5bae1def2a21eaf2ea4534fa8fef82984772ecafc19e8.png)

![step4_starbie_3d_angle](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/SbrkIUQC9RUO8DToeavOMkE0vX78Rnig/f81c098895715a341aa9698352aac6b8337ba17b8d95a6560aa06072c2796c09.png)

  Final stretch! Exported all the Gerber files and the drill file into a zip (Starbie-gerbers.zip) ready to send off to get manufactured.

  Then grabbed the Arduino sketch (Starbie.ino) into the Firmware folder and even messed around with the little HTML simulator in the browser. Starbie walks
  around, naps, and sends up hearts.

I'm officially done!
